California Fruit Sales.
August 11, 600
California Fruit Sales.
CHICAGO, August 11th. — The Montgomery Auction Company sold to day for Gregory Bros. Company, W. K. Strong Company and the Earl Fruit Company, seven carloads of California fruit. Foster peaches sold for $14 to $14; to Early Crawford peaches, $16 to $13; Orange clings, $15 to $12; Lemon Clings, $12; Susquehannas, $10 to $10; Bartlett pears, $14 to $13; Howells, $9 to $9; Muscats, half crates, $25 to $19; Tokays, half crates, $30 to $31; Blue Malvoe, $14; Ostrinbeam, half crates, $16; Chasseals, half crates, $14; Collar plums, $16 to $15; Purple plums, $15; Goldendrop plums, $12; Washington plums, $12; Gross plums, $18 to $16; nectarines, $12.

Sugar Tests.
NEW YORK, August 11th. — A special from Washington says that as a result of the protest by Spreckels c necerning the difference of classification in mat and bag sugar between New York and Philadelphia, it has been decided to make the test at New York the same as at Philadelphia. The practice has been at Philadelphia that where more than two tests of a given sample were made, to accept the average of all the tests made. The practice at New York has been to accept for classification the test most nearly coinciding with the average only of the lower tests found for each sample.

WASHINGTON, August 11th. — The population of Kansas City, as enumerated by the Census Bureau to day, is 38,170. The same place in 1880 had 9,348, an increase in ten years of 28,-22.

Superintendent Porter expects the work of counting the population of the country will be completed before the end of the present month, and Congress, if it so desires, can proceed to pass an apportionment bill and so determine how many members shall constitute the next House. The population of the country is estimated at 64,000,000.

General Alger and Party.
SALEM (Mass.), August 11th. — General Alger received a warm welcome at Salem this afternoon at the hands of the Phil. H. Sheridan Pett and citizens generally. The Mayor welcomed Alger and his staff and the Vermont veterans. General Alger responded briefly. With General Alger were Mrs. Alger, Mrs. Logan, Mrs. Mrs. Senator Stockbridge, Miss Alger and Miss Platt.

New Postoffice.

WASHINGTON, August 11th.—A new postoffice has been established at Lakeview, Ormsby county, Nevada, with H. M. Hobart as Postmaster.

Clarkson Resigns.

WASHINGTON, August 11th—First Assistant Postmaster-General Clarkson to-day tendered to the President his resignation, to take effect September 1st next.

Fatal Quarrel.

HOUSTON (Tex.), August 11th.—At Pattison, to-day, Charles and Daniel Ellison, brothers, killed each other during a quarrel.

LYNCHED A NEGRO.
He Tried to Assault Two Women—Taken from the Sheriff by a Mob.

ARKANSAS CITY, Ark., Aug. 11.—On last Friday morning a negro, 20 years of age, named William Beaver, living with Mr. Abernathy near Warren, Bradford county, attempted to assault Miss Inez Abernathy while the young lady was gathering eggs in her father's lot. She fought the fellow off and screamed, bringing her mother from the house to her assistance. The negro fled. That evening he made a similar attempt upon a negro girl near Mr. Sutton's plantation. He was unsuccessful this time also.

On Friday night, news of the man's attempt upon Miss Abernathy becoming known, a posse of men was organized to arrest him. On Sunday evening he was captured by Sheriff Watson and a deputy sheriff a few miles from Warren. The officers started to jail with their prisoner, but were met by an armed mob who took Beaver away from Watson, locked the Sheriff and his deputy up in jail, and swung the negro to a limb. This morning the body was found dangling at the end of a rope on the public square.

DANGLING AT A ROPE'S END.
A Colored Brute Lynched by a Mob.
ARKANSAS CITY, Ark., Aug. 11.—Last Friday morning a negro boy about twenty years of age, named William Beaver, living with Mr. Abernathy, near Warren, Bradley county, assaulted and attempted to outrage Miss Inez Abernathy while the young lady was gathering up eggs in her father's lot. She fought the brute off and screamed, bringing her mother from the house to her assistance. The negro fled without having accomplished his purpose. That evening he met and made a similar assault upon a negro girl near Mr. Sutton's plantation. He was unsuccessful this time also. Friday night news of the fiend's assault upon Miss Abernathy becoming known, a posse of men was organized to arrest him. Sunday evening he was captured by Sheriff Watson and a deputy sheriff a few miles from Warren. The officers started to jail with their prisoner, but were met by an armed mob of some eight or ten men, who took Beaver away from Watson, locked the sheriff and his deputy up in jail and swung the negro to a limb. This morning the body of the would-be rapist was found dangling to the end of a rope on the public square.

Beaver's Case Soon Settled.
SEKANAS CITY, Ark. Aug. 13.
ARKANSAS CITY, Ark., Aug. 13.—A negro named William Beaver attacked Mra. Lucy Abernathy last Friday, but she beat him off and he fled. On the evening of the same day Beaver made a similar attack upon a colored girl and was arrested. Later in the evening a crowd of men took him away from the sheriff and hanged him to a tree.

PERSONAL. Mrs. Robert T. Lincoln and her daughters have sailed from London for New York. Minister Lincoln will follow his family to America in November, to be absent from his post six weeks. Arthur Krupp of Germany, cousin of the famous manufacturer of cannon and himself famous as an extensive hardware manufacturer, has arrived in New York. He will make an extensive tour through the United States to study its iron industry and will attend the convention of German and English iron founders and engineers. ACCIDENTAL.
ACCIDENTAL.

The Hungarian town of Moor has been almost totally destroyed by fire. Ten persons lost their lives.

The floods in Hungary continue. The harvest is ruined. Many houses have been wrecked and a number of lives have been lost.

Seven persons were killed by the bursting of the steam pipe on the Russian man-of-war Tehesma the other day. Among the victims was Prince Khilkoff.

A boiler in John Jacoby's saw mill at Mulberry Ind., exploded, kil ling Will Shoemaker, and injuring John Jacoby, Allen Jacoby, Mont Rhodes and two children of Alfred Collins.

The British steamer Halcyon collided with the British steamer Rheubin near Sligo, Spain. The Halcyon sank. Thirteen persons were drowned.

SINS AND SINNERS.

Eyrand, the notorious French murderer in prison in Paris, tore his shirt into strips and had nearly strangled himself when discovered.

Near Arkansas City, Kan., a negro boy named William Beaver, who had attempted to assault two girls, was hanged by a mob. The sheriff and deputy were locked in the jail until the lynching was over.

The accounts of Girard Austin, treasurer of San Jose county, Colo., who died May 3, have been found short $17,000. The shortage is due to carelessness, and will be ma de good by his bondsm en.

A party of rebel Arabs met and defeated the Morocco army at Atinsi with considerable loss. One hundred and twenty captives taken by the rebels were put to death. The son of the governor was compelled to eat toasted portions of his own flesh.

J. S. Colemesnit, who was in the service of the United States government in Samoa during President Cleveland's administration, and who gained considerable notoriety during the late Samoan troubles, is wanted in Seattle, Wash., for forgery.

Dr. O. Sawyer of Chicago was shot and probably fatally injured by J. Bart on Sancher, correspondent of the Chicago Horseman. Sancher claims to have secured confessions that the doctor and Mrs. Sancher were intimate.

Sheriff Isaac Wright has arrived in Kokomo, Ind., from Fort Worth, Tex., having in charge Freeman Cooper, the absconding lawyer who skipped a few weeks ago, leaving $17,750 in forged notes on which he had collected the money. There are twenty-four indictments against him.

A feud has existed for years between a family named Ganday and another named Fairchild, at Meridian, Miss., and two Gandy boys met two of the Fairchilds in Tuscanola. A fight ensued, with knives, in which Brown Gandy was supposed to have received fatal wounds, and one of the Fairchilds is seriously cut and there is little hope of his recovery.

George Simpson, a well known jeweler of Phillipsburg, Mont., received news that his fourteen-year old daughter had been abducted from St. Peter's mission, near Cascade. The girl's mother and a young man with foreign accent are the abductors. When the mother superior tried to prevent the abduction the man drew a revolver and fired a shot, which frightened the nuns, and the couple proceeded unmolested. No trace as yet has been found of them.
